newsitem.title: UK: Britain ups N.Irish security funds as peace wanes.
newsitem.headline: Britain ups N.Irish security funds as peace wanes.

text.p: Britain on Tuesday confirmed fears that it sees peace as a distance prospect in Northern Ireland by announcing a large increase in spending on security in the province.
After two years of comparative peace in Northern Ireland, Britain's minister for the province, Sir Patrick Mayhew, said "law and order" had once more become his top priority.
"The peace dividend has, alas, been reversed, and this has obviously had an adverse effect on the provision of public services in Northern Ireland," Mayhew told a news conference.

He said the government was allocating an extra 120 million pounds ($198 million) over the next three years to policing and compensation. It brings security spending for the province in the next financial year to more than 930 million pounds.

The Irish Republican Army (IRA) has carried out a series of bombings on the British mainland since it abandoned a 17-month truce in February, but has so far launched only one attack in Northern Ireland -- on Britain's main army base.
But grumbling sectarian strife remains an enormous problem.
Traditional Protestant marches in towns and villages across the province have sparked off a series of violent clashes and riots between the rival communities since the summer.
One such wave of incidents in Drumcree earlier this year caused damage of 40 million pounds.
"This constitutes a grievous and wanton self-inflicted wound on the people of this province," Mayhew said.
In the largely Protestant town of Ballymena, police have had to protect Catholic churgoers against pro-British "loyalist" demonstrators for the past 13-weeks.
Meanwhile, the IRA has been reported as saying it will eschew its traditional Christmas truce this year, and police are stepping up security across the province.

The IRA has not carried out any attacks since its bombing of the Lisburn barracks south of Belfast in October, raising speculation it was operating an unofficial ceasefire to win favours for its political arm Sinn Fein.

But British Prime Minister John Major on Monday stood firm in his refusal to allow Sinn Fein immediate access to talks on the future of Northern Ireland if the IRA called a new truce in its battle for a united Ireland.

Major's Irish counterpart, John Bruton, made clear he wanted Sinn Feininvolved as soon as possible and suggested the Christmas recess in the talks chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell would give the IRA time to show it had called a genuine ceasefire.
The issue has caused a rift between London and Dublin which together forged the peace process three years ago in an attempt to end a quarter of a century of sectarian strife.
Major effectively is in a minority in the British parliament, forcing him to depend heavily on Northern Irish unionist politicians for support.

The Protestant unionists are determined to keep Northern Ireland under British rule and could withdraw their cooperation if they believe Major has granted any concessions to Sinn Fein. ($1=.6047 Pound)
